fifoPage.seoTitle: FIFO capital gains calculator: stocks & crypto | TrimmTrack
fifoPage.seoDesc: Free FIFO calculator for realized gains and losses when you sell stocks or crypto bought in several lots. Enter your buys and sells in order and get the result per sale, remaining shares and average cost.
fifoPage.lead: When you buy the same asset in several lots and later sell part of it, the taxable result is worked out with the FIFO method: the earliest shares you bought are sold first. Enter your trades in chronological order and the calculator gives you the realized gain or loss for each sale, the shares you have left and their average cost.
fifoPage.whatBody: FIFO (First In, First Out) is the rule that decides which shares count as sold when you have buys at different prices. Under FIFO, a sale always consumes the oldest shares you still hold open. It is the method most tax authorities apply to shares, and the most common convention for crypto too.
fifoPage.howBody: For each sale, the calculator walks your buys from oldest to newest and takes shares until the sold quantity is covered. The gain or loss is the difference between the sell price and the buy price of each lot consumed. If a sale exceeds the shares available, it warns you. The total realized is the sum of all sales.
fifoPage.exampleBody: You buy 10 shares at €100 and then 10 more at €120. If you sell 15 at €130, FIFO consumes the first 10 (gain 10 × €30 = €300) and then 5 of the second lot (gain 5 × €10 = €50): a realized result of €350. You are left with 5 shares at an average cost of €120.

what.a: To know how much you gained or lost when you sell part of a position bought at different prices, using the FIFO method. It is the figure you report as a capital gain or loss and the one that goes in the «Result» column of your spreadsheet.

crypto.a: Yes. The calculation is identical for stocks, ETFs or crypto: enter the buys and sells of any asset in order and the calculator applies FIFO the same way.

partial.q: What if I only sell part of the position?
partial.a: It handles that automatically. It consumes the oldest lots until the sale is covered and shows you the shares you have left open and their average cost, so you can keep tracking.

tax.q: Is this the figure I have to declare?
tax.a: FIFO is the method tax authorities use for shares, but a tax return can have specifics (fees, withholdings, wash-sale rules). Use this tool as a calculation aid, not as tax advice.

forecast.seoTitle: ETF portfolio forecast & simulation calculator | TrimmTrack
forecast.title: ETF Simulator
forecast.subtitle: Project how a passive/ETF portfolio could grow with recurring contributions, fees and an uncertainty band (Monte Carlo). Not a prediction — a range of scenarios.
forecast.disclaimer: Educational simulation of 1,500 Monte Carlo scenarios over your assumptions. Past or expected returns don't guarantee future results. Not financial advice.

guide.title: Key concepts for investing in ETFs
guide.intro: Before playing with the simulator, these are the principles that truly decide long-term results. None of them is a secret — the hard part is sticking to them for decades.

lowCost.title: Low fees (TER)
lowCost.body: Fees eat into your return every single year, whatever the market does. A global index ETF shouldn't cost more than 0.20% a year: if you're being charged more, that's a red flag — cheaper equivalents exist. Try the simulator with a 0.2% vs 1.5% TER and watch the difference compound into tens of thousands over 20 years.

keepBuying.title: Keep buying — especially through the drops
keepBuying.body: You've probably heard that anyone who invested at the 2000 peak didn't break even until 2013. That's misleading: it's only true for a single lump sum. Anyone who kept buying every month accumulated shares at the cheap 2001–2003 and 2008–2009 prices and returned to profit years earlier, with a far better return. Downturns are when your contributions buy cheap.

diversify.title: Diversify properly: go global
diversify.body: A single world-index ETF (MSCI World or ACWI) gives you thousands of companies across dozens of countries in one purchase. Betting on one sector, one country or the theme of the moment concentrates risk — and historically most of those bets end up underperforming the global index.

accumulating.title: Accumulating beats distributing
accumulating.body: An accumulating ETF reinvests dividends automatically: compounding works with zero effort and without paying tax each year on distributed dividends. If you don't need the income, accumulating share classes are usually more tax-efficient and more convenient.

stayInvested.title: Time in the market > timing the market
stayInvested.body: Nobody knows when markets will fall or recover. The best market days tend to cluster right next to the worst ones: panic-sellers usually miss them, and missing just a handful of the best days over 20 years wrecks the outcome. Volatility isn't a flaw in the plan — it's the price you pay for the return.

quality.title: Pick large, physically replicated funds
quality.body: Before buying, check three things: assets under management (ideally above €100M, lowers closure risk), physical replication (the fund actually holds the shares) and the tracking difference versus the index — the real all-in cost once everything is added up.

guide.note: Educational content, not personalised financial advice.

performance.title: Performance
performance.irrHint: Internal rate of return (XIRR): the real annualised return your money has earned, accounting for WHEN you put each euro in and took it out. It's the textbook money-weighted measure. Unlike “Total return” (cumulative), IRR is a % per year.
performance.sinceHint: Total gain = unrealized gain (open) + realized result + dividends + interest. The % return is computed over net capital invested (all buys minus all sells) — the money you actually put in from your pocket, not capital recycled from one trade into another.
performance.needsBackfill: To see the % return for each year you need to download the price history.
performance.byYearHint: “Return %” and “Value gain” reconstruct the portfolio's market value at year-end (includes unrealized gains, ~3 years of history). “Realized €” is closed sales + dividends + interest for that year, exact across all history.

fundamentals.perCardHint: Portfolio average P/E (price/earnings), weighted by each position's value and computed as a harmonic mean (the correct way to aggregate ratios). Uses the trailing P/E from fundamentals; crypto and unprofitable companies are left out.

dcf.intro: Projects the per-share metric (EPS or FCF/share), applies an exit multiple and discounts the future price at your desired return. The fair value is the most you can pay today to earn that return.
dcf.missing: No base {{metric}} available from Yahoo. Enter it manually or refresh fundamentals.
dcf.negative: Base {{metric}} is negative or zero: this model doesn't apply (no positive earnings/FCF). Try the other metric or the scenarios.
dcf.reverseIntro: The inverse: starting from the current price, what annual growth must the company deliver to justify it given your multiple and return? A great sanity check.
dcf.reverseUnsolvable: Can't solve the implied growth with these assumptions (invalid price, multiple or base metric).
dcf.reverseSentence: The current price implies the market expects {{implied}}%/yr {{metric}} growth for {{years}} years. Do you think that's achievable?
dcf.reverseCompare: You assume {{assumed}}%/yr in the DCF → the market is {{verdict}} than your thesis.

graham.intro: Benjamin Graham's classic interest-adjusted formula. Fast and defensive, built for screening — not a fine valuation.
graham.missing: No EPS available from Yahoo. Enter it manually or refresh fundamentals.
graham.negative: EPS is negative or zero: Graham's formula doesn't apply to unprofitable companies.
graham.screenNote: Conservative screening estimate, not a precise valuation.
graham.clampNote: growth capped at {{cap}}% (the 2g term over-inflates at high growth)

mc.intro: Simulates thousands of DCF runs varying growth and exit multiple. Instead of one number you get a distribution of the {{metric}} fair value.
mc.pointHint: DCF central points: growth {{growth}}%, multiple {{multiple}}× (edit them in the DCF tab)
mc.sentence: The fair value is between {{p10}} and {{p90}} with ~80% probability.

sotp.intro: Value each stake the holding owns and sum them. Listed stakes pull a live market cap from Yahoo (× your stake); unlisted ones use a manual value. Holdings persistently trade below NAV: apply a holding discount so the target price is realistic.

analytics.title: Portfolio analytics

analytics.disclaimer: Computed over {{weeks}} weeks with your current allocation applied retrospectively. Covers {{pct}}% of portfolio value.
analytics.tipBeta: Sensitivity of the portfolio to the market. Beta=1 means it moves with the benchmark; >1 more volatile, <1 less.
analytics.tipAlpha: Excess return that isn't explained by market risk. Positive alpha = portfolio beats what its risk would predict.
analytics.tipSharpe: Return per unit of total risk. >1 is good, >2 excellent, <0 means risk-free would have been better.
analytics.tipVolatility: Annualised standard deviation of returns. Higher = bigger swings.
analytics.tipMaxDD: Worst peak-to-trough drop in the analysis window. A measure of the historical worst case.
analytics.tipRSquared: How much of the portfolio's movement is explained by the market (0-100%). 100% = identical to benchmark.
analytics.tipExcluded: Tickers with under 6 months of history or no Yahoo data. Their weight is redistributed to the included ones.

warnings.two-month-rule: Two-month rule: you repurchased {{detail}} shortly before or after selling at a loss. Those losses can't be deducted yet (they surface when you sell the repurchased shares).
warnings.model-720: With more than €50,000 at foreign institutions you probably need to file Modelo 720 (informative declaration of foreign assets). It has its own deadlines and penalties.
warnings.model-721: With more than €50,000 of crypto on foreign platforms you probably need to file Modelo 721.
warnings.crypto-regime: You sold crypto ({{detail}}): it's taxed the same way as capital gains (FIFO), but review its specific regime.
warnings.withholding-over-treaty: You were withheld €{{detail}} beyond the 15% the treaty allows: that excess isn't creditable in the return — it's reclaimed from the source country.
warnings.no-w8ben-hint: For US securities, file a W-8BEN with your broker so the withholding drops from 30% to 15%.
warnings.undated-events: {{detail}} undated operations couldn't be assigned to any tax year and were left out. Add the dates to the Excel to include them.

taxes.disclaimer: TrimmTrack is not a tax advisor and this report is orientative and educational only: it is not tax or legal advice. Always verify amounts and boxes in Renta Web or with a professional.
taxes.whatBody: It takes your trades (from your TrimmTrack portfolio or an Excel) and computes what the return needs: the net balance of FIFO gains and losses on disposals, investment income (dividends and interest), cross-offsetting with the 25% cap, the international double-taxation credit and an estimated tax over the savings brackets. It also automatically flags cases people miss, like the two-month rule or the Modelo 720 thresholds.
taxes.howBody: Pick country and tax year, load your data, review the detected operations, answer four optional questions and get the report with every amount and its orientative Renta Web box. Everything is computed in your browser: upload an Excel without an account and nothing is stored anywhere.

casella.q: Which boxes of the Spanish return do shares and dividends go in?
casella.a: Orientatively: dividends go under investment income (box 0029), interest in 0027, sales of listed shares under capital gains (boxes 0328 onwards) and the international double-taxation credit in 0588. Numbers can shift between years — always confirm in Renta Web.

fifo.q: How is the gain on a share sale computed?
fifo.a: With the FIFO rule: the shares you bought first are deemed sold first. The gain is the sale value minus the acquisition cost of those specific shares. The assistant computes it automatically for every sale.

foreign.q: What about foreign dividends and double withholding?
foreign.a: The source country withholds a part (usually up to 15% by treaty) and Spain also taxes the dividend. In the return you can credit the foreign withholding up to the treaty cap. If more was withheld (e.g. the US 30% without a W-8BEN), the excess is reclaimed from the source country, not in the return.

advice.a: No. It's an informative, educational tool that helps you prepare the data. The final result is computed by Renta Web, and complex situations call for a professional tax advisor.

xray.whatTitle: What does the X-ray look at?
xray.whatBody: The grade blends four signals: how many effective positions you hold (concentration), the breadth of the portfolio, geographic exposure and, when data is available, the sector mix. On top we add total return, IRR and a list of concrete risks like concentration in a single position, region or currency. It's a starting point to think, not a recommendation.

what.q: What do I need to use it?
what.a: The Excel exported from your broker in TrimmTrack's format, or simply the ticker, shares and average price of each holding typed by hand.

privacy.a: Nowhere. The Excel is read inside your browser and holdings are never stored on the server. We only look up public prices to value them.

grade.a: We combine concentration (effective holdings), the number of positions, exposure by region and the sector mix into a 0–100 score, mapped to a letter from A+ to F.

free.a: Yes, and no sign-up. If you want to track the portfolio live with prices, dividends and valuations, you can create a free account.

xray.disclaimer: This X-ray is an educational tool, not financial advice. Prices are public and may be delayed.

stats.impliedGrowth: Annual growth the price is pricing in

notes.dcf: Fair value = EPS × (1+g)^n × exit multiple, discounted back at your required return. A positive upside means the model sees the stock as undervalued at today's price.
notes.reverse: Reverse DCF solves the forward model for growth: given the price, exit multiple and the return you demand, what constant EPS growth would the market have to be assuming? Compare it with the company's realistic growth to judge whether expectations are rich or cheap.
notes.graham: V = EPS × (8.5 + 2g) × 4.4 / Y, the interest-rate-adjusted revision. It's a fast, conservative screen — not a precise valuation.
notes.grahamCapped: Growth was capped at {{cap}}% because the linear 2g term over-inflates above that.
notes.compound: Assumes contributions are added at the end of each month and the return compounds monthly. A real ETF return varies year to year — use the Monte Carlo simulator to see the range.
notes.mcRuns: {{runs}} simulations of the fair value distribution.
